cemc-euclid-2009-01a.title: Use two points
cemc-euclid-2009-01a.body:
The points $(0, 7)$ and $(1, 5)$ lie on the line (check: $0 + 21 - 21 = 0$ and $6 + 15 - 21 = 0$). Slope $= \frac{5 - 7}{1 - 0} = -2$.

**Answer: $-2$**

cemc-euclid-2009-01b.title: Rise over run
cemc-euclid-2009-01b.body:
Slope $3$ means $3$ units up for every unit right. From $x = 1$ to $x = 5$ is $4$ units right, so we go $12$ units up from $y = 0$: $c = 12$.

**Answer: 12**

cemc-euclid-2009-01c.title: Equation of the line
cemc-euclid-2009-01c.body:
The slope of $AB$ is $\frac{-4 - 4}{8 - 0} = -1$ and its $y$-intercept is $4$, so the line is $y = -x + 4$. Then $(k, k)$ on it gives $k = -k + 4$, so $k = 2$.

**Answer: $k = 2$**

cemc-euclid-2009-01c.title: Equal slopes
cemc-euclid-2009-01c.body:
Let $K = (k, k)$. The slope of $AK$ must equal the slope of $AB$, which is $-1$: $\frac{k - 4}{k} = -1$, so $k - 4 = -k$ and $k = 2$.

**Answer: $k = 2$**

cemc-euclid-2009-02a.title: Factor
cemc-euclid-2009-02a.body:
$x^2 - 6x - 7 = (x - 7)(x + 1) = 0$, so the roots are $7$ and $-1$, with sum $6$.

**Answer: 6**

cemc-euclid-2009-02a.title: Sum of roots
cemc-euclid-2009-02a.body:
For $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ the sum of the roots is $-\frac{b}{a} = -\frac{-6}{1} = 6$.

**Answer: 6**

cemc-euclid-2009-02b.title: Product of roots
cemc-euclid-2009-02b.body:
For $ax^2 + bx + c = 0$ the product of the roots is $\frac{c}{a} = \frac{-20}{5} = -4$.

**Answer: $-4$**

cemc-euclid-2009-02c.title: Factor
cemc-euclid-2009-02c.body:
$x^3 - 6x^2 + 5x = x(x^2 - 6x + 5) = x(x - 1)(x - 5)$, so the roots are $0, 1, 5$, with average $\frac{6}{3} = 2$.

**Answer: 2**

cemc-euclid-2009-02c.title: Sum of roots of a cubic
cemc-euclid-2009-02c.body:
For $ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d = 0$ the three roots sum to $-\frac{b}{a} = 6$ (and here they are distinct, as $x^2 - 6x + 5$ has roots $1, 5 \ne 0$). The average is $\frac63 = 2$.

**Answer: 2**

cemc-euclid-2009-03a.title: Angles in the isosceles triangles
cemc-euclid-2009-03a.body:
$\triangle ABD$ is equilateral, so $\angle ADB = 60^\circ$. In right triangle $AED$, $\angle DAE = 180^\circ - 60^\circ - 90^\circ = 30^\circ$, so $\angle CAD = 180^\circ - 30^\circ = 150^\circ$.

$\triangle CAD$ is isosceles ($AC = AD$), so $\angle CDA = \frac12(180^\circ - 150^\circ) = 15^\circ$.

Thus $\angle CDB = 15^\circ + 60^\circ = 75^\circ$.

**Answer: $75^\circ$**

cemc-euclid-2009-03a.title: Use triangle CBD
cemc-euclid-2009-03a.body:
By symmetry about line $CE$ (the perpendicular bisector of $BD$, since $\triangle ABD$ is equilateral), $\angle BCD = 2\angle ACD = 2 \cdot 15^\circ = 30^\circ$, where $\angle ACD = 15^\circ$ as found from isosceles $\triangle CAD$ with apex angle $150^\circ$.

$\triangle CBD$ is isosceles with $CB = CD$, so $\angle CDB = \frac12(180^\circ - 30^\circ) = 75^\circ$.

**Answer: $75^\circ$**

cemc-euclid-2009-03b.title: Area two ways
cemc-euclid-2009-03b.body:
$AB = CD = 40$ and $AD = BC = 30$, so $BD = \sqrt{30^2 + 40^2} = 50$.

The area of $\triangle ABD$ is $\frac12 \cdot 40 \cdot 30 = 600$, and also $\frac12 \cdot BD \cdot AF = 25x$. So $25x = 600$ and $x = 24$.

**Answer: $x = 24$**

cemc-euclid-2009-03b.title: Similar triangles / trigonometry
cemc-euclid-2009-03b.body:
$BD = 50$ as above. $\triangle BFA \sim \triangle BAD$ (both right-angled, common angle at $B$), so
$$\frac{AF}{AB} = \frac{AD}{BD} \implies \frac{x}{40} = \frac{30}{50} \implies x = 24.$$
(Equivalently, $\sin\angle ADB = \frac{40}{50} = \frac{x}{30}$.)

**Answer: $x = 24$**

cemc-euclid-2009-04a.title: Average of first and last
cemc-euclid-2009-04a.body:
The sum of an arithmetic sequence is (number of terms) $\times$ (average of first and last terms). With $n$ terms: $n \cdot \frac{1 + 19}{2} = 10n = 70$, so $n = 7$.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-euclid-2009-04a.title: Use the common difference
cemc-euclid-2009-04a.body:
With $n$ terms and difference $d$: $1 + (n - 1)d = 19$, so $(n - 1)d = 18$. The sum is $\frac{n}{2}\big(2 + (n - 1)d\big) = \frac n2 \cdot 20 = 10n = 70$, so $n = 7$ (and $d = 3$: $1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19$).

**Answer: 7**

cemc-euclid-2009-04b.title: Compare coefficients
cemc-euclid-2009-04b.body:
Expanding, $(a + ab)x + 3ab = 2x + 12$ for all $x$, so $a + ab = 2$ and $3ab = 12$. Then $ab = 4$, so $a = 2 - 4 = -2$ and $b = \frac{4}{-2} = -2$.

**Answer: $a = -2$, $b = -2$**

cemc-euclid-2009-05a.title: Drop the altitude
cemc-euclid-2009-05a.body:
Let $P$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $C$ to $AB$; it is the midpoint of $AB$ as the triangle is isosceles. $\triangle CDP$ is a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle, so $PD = \frac12 CD = \frac32$.

Then $AP = 8 - \frac32 = \frac{13}{2} = PB$, and $DB = PB - PD = \frac{13}2 - \frac32 = 5$.

**Answer: $BD = 5$**

cemc-euclid-2009-05a.title: Cosine law
cemc-euclid-2009-05a.body:
$\angle CDB = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$. In $\triangle CDB$:
$$49 = 9 + BD^2 - 2 \cdot 3 \cdot BD \cos 120^\circ = 9 + BD^2 + 3BD,$$
so $BD^2 + 3BD - 40 = 0$, i.e. $(BD - 5)(BD + 8) = 0$, and $BD = 5$.

**Answer: $BD = 5$**

cemc-euclid-2009-05b.title: Convert to sin A
cemc-euclid-2009-05b.body:
In a right triangle, $\sin B = \cos A$. So $2\cos A = \frac{3\sin A}{\cos A}$, i.e. $2\cos^2 A = 3\sin A$. Using $\cos^2 A = 1 - \sin^2 A$:
$$2\sin^2 A + 3\sin A - 2 = 0 \iff (2\sin A - 1)(\sin A + 2) = 0.$$
Since $|\sin A| \le 1$, $\sin A = \frac12$, and as $A$ is acute, $A = 30^\circ$.

**Answer: $30^\circ$**

cemc-euclid-2009-05b.title: Use the side lengths
cemc-euclid-2009-05b.body:
With sides $a = BC$, $b = CA$, $c = AB$: $\sin B = \frac bc$ and $\tan A = \frac ab$. So $\frac{2b}{c} = \frac{3a}{b}$, i.e. $2b^2 = 3ac$. Since $b^2 = c^2 - a^2$:
$$2c^2 - 3ac - 2a^2 = 0 \iff (c - 2a)(2c + a) = 0,$$
so $c = 2a$. A right triangle whose hypotenuse is twice the side opposite $A$ has $\sin A = \frac12$, so $A = 30^\circ$.

**Answer: $30^\circ$**

cemc-euclid-2009-06a.title: List digit multisets
Complement digits
cemc-euclid-2009-06a.body:
Replace each digit $d$ by $9 - d$. Digit sum $24$ becomes digit sum $27 - 24 = 3$ for three "deficits" $x, y, z \ge 0$. The number of solutions of $x + y + z = 3$ is $\binom{5}{2} = 10$; all are valid since each deficit $\le 3 \le 8$ keeps the hundreds digit $\ge 6 \ne 0$. Probability $\frac{10}{900} = \frac1{90}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{90}$**

cemc-euclid-2009-06b.title: Equal times to G
cemc-euclid-2009-06b.body:
Alice drives $1$ km per minute, so $GF = 45$ km. Let Bob's speed be $B$ km/h and $EG = d$ km. Bob covers $EG$ in $\frac13$ h, so $d = \frac B3$.

They reach $G$ at the same time: $\frac{d}{60} = \frac{45}{B}$, so $Bd = 2700$, i.e. $\frac{B^2}{3} = 2700$, $B^2 = 8100$, $B = 90$.

**Answer: 90 km/h**

cemc-euclid-2009-06b.title: Ratio of speeds
cemc-euclid-2009-06b.body:
Let $t$ be the time (in minutes) until they meet. Alice covers $EG$ in $t$ minutes and Bob covers it in $20$; Bob covers $GF$ in $t$ minutes and Alice covers it in $45$. So
$$\frac{v_B}{v_A} = \frac{t}{20} = \frac{45}{t} \implies t^2 = 900 \implies t = 30.$$
Hence $v_B = \frac{30}{20} \cdot 60 = 90$ km/h.

**Answer: 90 km/h**

cemc-euclid-2009-07a.title: Compare vertices
cemc-euclid-2009-07a.body:
$y = x^2 - 2x + 4 = (x - 1)^2 + 3$ has vertex $(1, 3)$. The translated parabola still has leading coefficient $1$ and roots $3, 5$, so it is $y = (x - 3)(x - 5) = (x - 4)^2 - 1$, with vertex $(4, -1)$.

Moving $(1, 3)$ to $(4, -1)$ is $3$ right and $4$ down: $p = 3$, $q = 4$.

**Answer: $p = 3$, $q = 4$**

cemc-euclid-2009-07a.title: Translate the equation
cemc-euclid-2009-07a.body:
The translated parabola is $y = (x - p - 1)^2 + 3 - q$. Its roots are $p + 1 \pm \sqrt{q - 3}$, which must be $4 \pm 1$. So $p + 1 = 4$ and $q - 3 = 1$: $p = 3$, $q = 4$.

**Answer: $p = 3$, $q = 4$**

cemc-euclid-2009-07b.title: Find the parabola, then subtract areas
cemc-euclid-2009-07b.body:
Let $A = (a, 0)$. $\triangle ABC$ has base $AC = 4 - a$ and height $4$, so $2(4 - a) = 4$ and $a = 2$.

The parabola is $y = k(x - 2)(x - 4)$ with $-4 = k(-2)(-4)$, so $k = -\frac12$. Its vertex is at $x = 3$: $D = \left(3, \frac12\right)$.

Enclose $\triangle BDC$ in the rectangle $0 \le x \le 4$, $-4 \le y \le \frac12$ (area $4 \cdot \frac92 = 18$) and remove three right triangles:
$$18 - \tfrac12 \cdot 3 \cdot \tfrac92 - \tfrac12 \cdot 1 \cdot \tfrac12 - \tfrac12 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 = 18 - \tfrac{27}{4} - \tfrac14 - 8 = 3.$$

**Answer: 3**

cemc-euclid-2009-07b.title: Shoelace formula
cemc-euclid-2009-07b.body:
As in the first solution, $A = (2, 0)$, the parabola is $y = -\frac12(x - 2)(x - 4)$ and $D = (3, \frac12)$.

With $B(0, -4)$, $D(3, \frac12)$, $C(4, 0)$:
$$\text{Area} = \tfrac12\left|0\left(\tfrac12 - 0\right) + 3(0 - (-4)) + 4\left(-4 - \tfrac12\right)\right| = \tfrac12|12 - 18| = 3.$$

**Answer: 3**

cemc-euclid-2009-08a.title: Areas and similar triangles
cemc-euclid-2009-08a.body:
Drop perpendiculars from $A$ to $E$ on $PQ$ and from $P$ to $F$ on $DC$. Then $ABQE$ and $PQCF$ are rectangles, so $PE = r - x$ and $DF = y - r$. Let $BQ = b$ and $QC = c$; then $AE = b$ and $PF = c$.

Equal areas: $\frac12(x + r)b = \frac12(r + y)c$, so $\frac{c}{b} = \frac{x + r}{r + y}$.

Since $AE \parallel PF$ and $A, P, D$ are collinear, $\triangle AEP \sim \triangle PFD$, so $\frac{AE}{PE} = \frac{PF}{DF}$, i.e. $\frac cb = \frac{y - r}{r - x}$.

Hence $\frac{x + r}{r + y} = \frac{y - r}{r - x}$, so $(r + x)(r - x) = (y + r)(y - r)$, i.e. $r^2 - x^2 = y^2 - r^2$, which gives $x^2 + y^2 = 2r^2$. ∎

(If $x = y$, the figure is a rectangle and $r = x = y$, so the identity holds trivially.)

cemc-euclid-2009-08a.title: Extend the legs to a triangle
cemc-euclid-2009-08a.body:
If $x = y$ the trapezoid is a rectangle, $r = x = y$, and the result is clear. Otherwise, say $x < y$ (the other case is symmetric). Extend $DA$ and $CB$ to meet at a point $O$. Since $AB \parallel PQ \parallel DC$, triangles $OAB$, $OPQ$, $ODC$ are similar with ratio $x : r : y$, so their areas are $kx^2$, $kr^2$, $ky^2$ for some constant $k > 0$.

The two regions of the trapezoid have areas $kr^2 - kx^2$ (between $AB$ and $PQ$) and $ky^2 - kr^2$ (between $PQ$ and $DC$). These are equal, so $r^2 - x^2 = y^2 - r^2$, i.e. $x^2 + y^2 = 2r^2$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2009-08b.title: Cosine law twice
cemc-euclid-2009-08b.body:
Since $AB$ is tangent at $A$, $\angle OAB = 90^\circ$ and $OB^2 = r^2 + p^2$.

In $\triangle ODC$ ($OD = DC = q$, $OC = r$): $r^2 = 2q^2 - 2q^2\cos\angle ODC$, so $\cos\angle ODC = \frac{2q^2 - r^2}{2q^2}$.

In $\triangle ODB$, $\angle ODB = \angle ODC$ and $DB = 2q$:
$$OB^2 = q^2 + 4q^2 - 2(q)(2q)\cdot\frac{2q^2 - r^2}{2q^2} = 5q^2 - 2(2q^2 - r^2) = q^2 + 2r^2.$$
So $r^2 + p^2 = q^2 + 2r^2$, i.e. $p^2 = q^2 + r^2$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2009-08b.title: Median length formula
cemc-euclid-2009-08b.body:
In $\triangle OBD$, $C$ is the midpoint of $BD$ (since $BC = CD = q$), so $OC$ is a median. By Apollonius' theorem,
$$OB^2 + OD^2 = 2\,OC^2 + 2\,BC^2 \implies OB^2 + q^2 = 2r^2 + 2q^2 \implies OB^2 = 2r^2 + q^2.$$
(Apollonius follows from the cosine law at $C$: the angles $\angle OCB$ and $\angle OCD$ are supplementary, so the cosine terms cancel when the two cosine-law equations are added.)

As $AB$ is tangent, $OB^2 = OA^2 + AB^2 = r^2 + p^2$. Therefore $r^2 + p^2 = 2r^2 + q^2$, i.e. $p^2 = q^2 + r^2$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2009-09a.title: Convert to base 2
cemc-euclid-2009-09a.body:
Let $y = \log_2 x$. Then $1 + \log_4 x = 1 + \frac y2$ and $\log_8 4x = \frac{2 + y}{3}$.

For a geometric sequence, (middle)$^2$ = (first)(third):
$$\left(1 + \tfrac y2\right)^2 = y \cdot \tfrac{2 + y}{3} \iff 12 + 12y + 3y^2 = 8y + 4y^2 \iff y^2 - 4y - 12 = 0,$$
so $(y - 6)(y + 2) = 0$, giving $y = 6$ or $y = -2$, i.e. $x = 64$ or $x = \frac14$.

Check: $x = 64$ gives $6, 4, \frac83$ (ratio $\frac23$); $x = \frac14$ gives $-2, 0, 0$ (ratio $0$).

**Answer: $x = 64$ or $x = \frac14$**

cemc-euclid-2009-09b.title: Rotation
cemc-euclid-2009-09b.body:
Rotate $\triangle PSU$ by $90^\circ$ about $P$ so that $S$ goes to $Q$; let $U$ go to $V$, which lies on line $RQ$ extended beyond $Q$, with $QV = SU$ and $PV = PU$.

Then $\angle VPT = \angle VPQ + \angle QPT = \angle UPS + \angle QPT = 90^\circ - 45^\circ = 45^\circ = \angle UPT$. So $\triangle PTU \cong \triangle PTV$ (SAS), giving $UT = TV = TQ + SU$.

Perimeter of $\triangle RUT$ $= UR + RT + UT = UR + RT + TQ + SU = (SU + UR) + (RT + TQ) = 4 + 4 = 8$.

The perimeter is always $8$, so the maximum is $8$.

**Answer: 8**

cemc-euclid-2009-09b.title: Trigonometry
cemc-euclid-2009-09b.body:
Let $\angle SPU = \theta$ with $0^\circ \le \theta \le 45^\circ$ and $t = \tan\theta$. Then $SU = 4t$, $UR = 4 - 4t$, and $\angle QPT = 45^\circ - \theta$, so $QT = 4\cdot\frac{1 - t}{1 + t}$ and $RT = \frac{8t}{1 + t}$.

By Pythagoras, $UT^2 = 16\left[(1 - t)^2 + \frac{4t^2}{(1+t)^2}\right] = 16\cdot\frac{(1 - t^2)^2 + 4t^2}{(1 + t)^2} = 16\cdot\frac{(1 + t^2)^2}{(1 + t)^2}$, so $UT = \frac{4(1 + t^2)}{1 + t}$.

Perimeter $= \frac{4(1 - t^2) + 8t + 4(1 + t^2)}{1 + t} = \frac{8 + 8t}{1 + t} = 8$, for every $\theta$.

**Answer: 8**

cemc-euclid-2009-10a.title: Case on plate 1
cemc-euclid-2009-10a.body:
Write a placement as a string $p_1p_2\cdots p_7$ of $0$s and $1$s (with $p_7$ adjacent to $p_1$).

- $p_1 = 1$: then $p_2 = p_7 = 0$, and two non-adjacent $1$s go among $p_3p_4p_5p_6$: $1010100$, $1010010$, $1001010$ — $3$ ways.
- $p_1 = 0$, $p_2 = 1$: then $p_3 = 0$, and this is the previous case rotated by one plate — $3$ ways.
- $p_1 = p_2 = 0$: three non-adjacent $1$s among $p_3, \dots, p_7$ (and $p_7, p_1$ adjacency is fine): only $0010101$ — $1$ way.

Total $f(7, 3) = 7$.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-euclid-2009-10a.title: Rotations
cemc-euclid-2009-10a.body:
Three gifts on $7$ plates with no two adjacent: the gaps (numbers of empty plates between consecutive gifts going around) are positive and sum to $4$, so they are $1, 1, 2$ in some cyclic order. Up to rotation there is only one pattern, $1010100$, and it has no rotational symmetry (7 is prime), so it gives $7$ distinct rotations.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-euclid-2009-10b.title: Delete plates next to the end
cemc-euclid-2009-10b.body:
Number the plates $1, \dots, n$ around the table, and call a placement *valid* if no two neighbours both have gifts.

**Type 1:** plate $n$ is empty, and plates $n-1$ and $1$ are not both full. Removing plate $n$ (closing the circle so that $n-1$ and $1$ become neighbours) gives a valid placement of $k$ gifts on $n - 1$ plates. Conversely, inserting an empty plate between plates $n-1$ and $1$ of any valid $(n-1)$-placement gives a Type 1 placement. So there are $f(n-1, k)$ of Type 1.

**Type 2:** everything else, i.e. either (i) plate $n$ is full (so plates $n-1$ and $1$ are empty), or (ii) plate $n$ is empty and plates $n-1$ and $1$ are both full (so plate $n-2$ is empty). In both cases exactly one of plates $n-1, n$ is full. Remove plates $n-1$ and $n$, closing the circle so that $n-2$ and $1$ become neighbours. This leaves $k - 1$ gifts on $n - 2$ plates, and the placement is valid: in case (i) plate $1$ is empty; in case (ii) plate $n-2$ is empty.

Conversely, take a valid placement of $k - 1$ gifts on plates $1, \dots, n-2$. If plate $1$ is empty, insert plates $n-1$ (empty) and $n$ (full) — valid since plate $1$ and the new plate $n-1$ are empty; this gives case (i). If plate $1$ is full (so plate $n-2$ is empty), insert $n-1$ (full) and $n$ (empty) — valid since plate $n-2$ is empty; this gives case (ii). These maps are inverse to each other, so there are $f(n-2, k-1)$ placements of Type 2.

Therefore $f(n, k) = f(n-1, k) + f(n-2, k-1)$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2009-10b.title: Explicit formula
cemc-euclid-2009-10b.body:
Write a placement as a binary string $p_1\cdots p_n$ (with $p_n$ adjacent to $p_1$).

*Strings with $p_n = 0$:* every $1$ is followed by a $0$, so the string is a sequence of $k$ blocks "$10$" and $n - 2k$ blocks "$0$", and every such sequence is valid. There are $\binom{n-k}{k}$ of them.

*Strings with $p_n = 1$:* then $p_1 = p_{n-1} = 0$, and $p_2 \cdots p_{n-1}$ is a string of length $n - 2$ ending in $0$ with $k - 1$ ones and no two adjacent; as above there are $\binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ of them.

So $f(n, k) = \binom{n-k}{k} + \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$. Then, using Pascal's rule $\binom{m}{r} = \binom{m-1}{r} + \binom{m-1}{r-1}$ twice,
$$\begin{aligned}
f(n-1, k) + f(n-2, k-1) &= \tbinom{n-k-1}{k} + \tbinom{n-k-2}{k-1} + \tbinom{n-k-1}{k-1} + \tbinom{n-k-2}{k-2} \\
&= \left[\tbinom{n-k-1}{k} + \tbinom{n-k-1}{k-1}\right] + \left[\tbinom{n-k-2}{k-1} + \tbinom{n-k-2}{k-2}\right] \\
&= \tbinom{n-k}{k} + \tbinom{n-k-1}{k-1} = f(n, k). \ ∎
\end{aligned}$$

cemc-euclid-2009-10c.title: Product formula and the primes 7 and 41
cemc-euclid-2009-10c.body:
From $f(n,k) = \binom{n-k}{k} + \binom{n-k-1}{k-1}$ (see part (b)),
$$f(n, k) = \frac{(n-k-1)!\,\big[(n-k) + k\big]}{k!\,(n-2k)!} = \frac{n\,(n-k-1)(n-k-2)\cdots(n-2k+1)}{k!}.$$
The numerator is $n$ times $k - 1$ consecutive integers. $2009 = 7^2 \cdot 41$.

**Example.** $f(49, 5) = \frac{49 \cdot 43 \cdot 42 \cdot 41 \cdot 40}{120} = 49 \cdot 43 \cdot 14 \cdot 41$, a multiple of $2009$; $n + k = 54$.

**Minimality.** Suppose $2009 \mid f(n, k)$ with $n + k \le 53$; we derive a contradiction. Then $n \le 51$, every numerator factor is less than $82$, and so the factor $41$ must be $n$ itself or one of $n-k-1, \dots, n-2k+1$.

- *$n = 41$.* The other numerator factors are $k - 1$ consecutive integers, all at most $40 - k < 49$, so each contains at most one factor of $7$; among $k - 1$ consecutive integers there are at most $\lfloor \frac{k-1}{7} \rfloor + 1 \le \lfloor \frac k7 \rfloor + 1$ multiples of $7$, while $k!$ contains at least $\lfloor \frac k7 \rfloor$ factors of $7$. So $f(41, k)$ has at most one factor of $7$ — impossible.
- *$41$ is in the list.* Then $n - 2k + 1 \le 41 \le n - k - 1$, i.e. $42 + k \le n \le 40 + 2k$. With $n + k \le 53$ this gives $42 + 2k \le 53$, so $k \le 5$; hence $7 \nmid k!$ and the numerator itself needs $7^2$.
  - If $7 \mid n$: since $n \ge 42 + k \ge 44$ and $n \le 51$, $n = 49$; then $49 \le 40 + 2k$ gives $k \ge 5$ and $n + k \ge 54$, a contradiction.
  - If $7 \nmid n$: the list has $k - 1 \le 4$ consecutive integers, so at most one multiple of $7$, which must then be $49$; so $49 \le n - k - 1$, i.e. $n \ge 50 + k$, and $n + k \le 53$ gives $k \le 1$, a contradiction.

Hence the minimum is $54$.

**Answer: 54**
